findings.summary: The shared pinning helper handles struct data values, which fell through every branch unchanged before, so the return snapshot and the shared-return pin do what their contracts say for structs; the nullish site pins through it rather than through its own copy.

A struct held under a plain name is never pinned (the rule the receiver binding and the native-value description already use), so a search result or method result already in a local reads twice for free instead of being copied.

The nullish site pins only an operand whose presence flag is the derived one, spelled through one helper the leaf constructor shares; a flag another source supplied, such as a bounds test, selects the value once already and is left alone.

The pin re-derives only the spellings equal to the ones the leaf constructor derived from the original expression, without a dead delete arm; a supplied flag survives, which the metadata-carrying rebind idiom would have overwritten.
A bound method receiver re-derives its identity and presence spellings from the binding, so an optional method call on a popped instance pops once; the guard test expects the binding to be tested.

The fixture asserts only shapes that can fail: shift and pop under the operator, an inlined nullable return, two calls of a state-changing struct-returning function, and an optional method call on a popped instance; the effect-free at, the empty-array find and the scalar shift the widening fixture already covers are gone.
The leaf constructor could mark the spellings it derives so pinning and the receiver binding stop comparing against a second leaf, or stop storing derived spellings at all behind a presence helper.
findings.blockedBy: Every reader of the two derived spellings (about forty-five presence checks and the identity comparisons) would change with them, and no measurement shows which of the two designs keeps the generated tree neutral; the comparison against a second leaf is exact today.
